Discover What You Know
Learning Objectives
Define general biomechanics terminology.
Describe kinematic motion of the tibiofemoral and patellofemoral knee joint.
Discuss healthy tibiofemoral and patellofemoral joint loading patterns and alterations in
loading from injury.
Explain the role of joint replacement in restoring knee joint mechanics.
Review tribology and wear mechanisms.
Knee Joint Kinematics
Kinematics is the field within classical mechanics that describes the motion of objects without
regard to their mass or how their motion is brought about.



In general, kinematics is concerned with the geometric and time-dependent aspects of
motion, without considering the forces or moments responsible for the motion.
Kinematics principally involves the relationships between position, velocity, and acceleration.
The knee is a triarticular joint, with two tibiofemoral compartments and a patellofemoral
joint.
Tibiofemoral Kinematics
Overview
The term kinematics of the knee joint describes motion in the sagittal, transverse, and frontal
planes.
The greatest range of motion (ROM) occurs in the sagittal plane (approximately 160°).
Motion in the transverse and frontal planes is linked to the position of the joint in the sagittal
plane. ROM increases as knee flexion increases, reaching a maximum at 90° of flexion.
In the transverse plane, knee rotation ranges from 45° in external rotation to 30° in internal
rotation.
In the frontal plane, ROM in abduction and adduction reaches a maximum of 10°.
During walking, knee excursions in the sagittal, frontal, and transverse planes reach
approximately 70°, 15°, and 10°, respectively.
More extreme motion, such as squatting, requires knee flexion of as much as 160° and
external rotation of as much as 20°.
In vivo investigations have demonstrated that substantial angular and linear motions occur
about all six degrees of freedom of the joint during activities of daily living. In general, the
motion pattern is activity specific.
Ligaments and anatomic surface features provide the constraints that define the envelope of
knee motion during various activities.
Studies1-3show that rupture of the cruciate ligaments or disruption of the tibiofemoral
surface, including the menisci, causes a major change in knee kinematics, leading to articular
dysfunction.
Successful total knee arthroplasty (TKA) relies on proper positioning of the components to
restore proper knee kinematics.
If no force is applied during knee flexion, the knee joint progresses with a combination of
rolling and sliding posteriorly4 (Figure 1). Anterior slip during knee flexion has been termed
paradoxical motion.

https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000552
2/19

The slip velocity between the condyle and the tibial plateau of a TKA implant can quantify the
degree of rolling and sliding of the tibiofemoral joint surfaces across one another. This factor
has implications for joint lubrication.
Figure 1 Schematic drawing of a knee shows the three fundamental motions that occur between
the articular surfaces. The point of contact changes on both articular surfaces during rolling
motion. The point of contact on the moving surface remains constant during sliding motion. A
single point of contact occurs on the fixed surface during spinning motion. Some joints, such as
the tibiofemoral joint, experience all three of these motions simultaneously. (Reproduced with
permission from Gustafson JA, Takenaga T, Debski RE: Basic concepts in functional biomechanics,
in Musahl V, Karlsson J, Krutsch W, Mandelbaum B, Espregueira-Mendes J, d’Hooghe P, eds:
Return to Play in Football. Berlin, Germany, Springer, 2018, pp 3-15.)

Overview
Experiments demonstrating the rolling and sliding mechanism were conducted as early
as 1836 by the Weber brothers. They evaluated the relative motion between the femoral
condyles and the tibial surface by placing markers on the corresponding points of
contact on both surfaces.5 Nearly 100 years later, the ratio of rolling to sliding was
demonstrated to vary during flexion and extension.6 Rolling predominates early in
flexion (0° to 20°), whereas sliding becomes dominant at flexion angles beyond 30°.7 This
mechanism is called femoral rollback. One of the models designed to explain this
mechanism is the crossed four-bar linkage, considered by Müller8 as well as O’Connor
and Zavatsky.9 In this model, the insertions of both cruciate ligaments are attached
rigidly to the femur and the tibia. They are represented by two crossed bars, which are
not linked but held fixed firmly at their anatomic points of insertion (Resource 1).
Stability and freedom of movement are adjusted via the mechanistic interplay between
the shape of the articulating surfaces and the passive and active soft-tissue structures.
The geometry of the joint surfaces and the soft-tissue constraints determine the
kinematic behavior of the knee. As the knee is rolling on a larger curvature laterally than
medially, it moves a greater distance on the lateral plateau than on the medial plateau.
9/3/26, 7:30 AM
AAOS | Biomechanics of the Knee
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000552
3/19

As a result, the femur not only moves posteriorly during rollback but also rotates
externally during flexion. The reverse situation, as the knee extends and the femur
internally rotates, is called the screw-home mechanism, locking the lower extremities to
a solid column. The asymmetric attachment of the menisci contributes to this motion
pattern. The lateral meniscus is much more mobile than the medial meniscus. This factor
is compatible with a greater movement on the lateral side than on the medial side. The
more rigid attachment of the medial meniscus serves as a secondary restraint to
anterior movement of the tibia, providing more stability to the joint.
Kinematics During Gait
Typically, flexion and extension are highly reproducible in the same individual during human
locomotion in healthy subjects and in patients who undergo TKA. More variability is present in
secondary kinematics (ie, anteroposterior translation, internal-external rotation).
Patients who undergo TKA show gait adaptations, with movement patterns that deviate from
normal. This is true for posterior-stabilized and cruciate-retaining designs.

Kinematics During Gait
During level walking, the knee is extended almost fully at heel strike. After heel strike,
the knee begins to bend, reaching a maximum of approximately 15° to 20° of knee
flexion during midstance. At this point, the direction of the angular progression reverses,
and the knee fully extends again (approximately 45% of gait cycle). The joint reverses
direction again to start the pre-swing phase and continues flexion into toe-off, which
occurs at approximately 63% of the gait cycle.
In patients who undergo TKA, deficits often are observed at heel strike, at which full
extension may not be reached. In addition, midstance extension typically is not as
pronounced as that observed during normal gait. A multitude of radio-fluoroscopy
studies have assessed the secondary kinematics for various TKA implant designs.10 In
general, TKA kinematics may not follow the translational and rotational patterns of the
natural knee. In particular, some cruciate-retaining designs have shown paradoxical
anterior femoral translation during early knee flexion, whereas few posterior-stabilized
9/3/26, 7:30 AM
AAOS | Biomechanics of the Knee
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000552
4/19

designs are prone to paradoxical translation because of post/cam engagement;
however, the latter limits natural knee rotation, which is larger but variable in cruciate-
retaining knees. The most natural knee kinematics have been observed with bicruciate-
retaining TKA; however, few differences have been found between the outcomes of
bicruciate designs and other designs.10
Using skin markers for motion tracking, Dyrby and Andriacchi11 found that, relative to a
fixed femur, the tibia moves posteriorly after heel strike and changes direction at
approximately 15% to 20% of the gait cycle to translate anteriorly. Therefore, only the
portion after midstance would be consistent with a femoral rollback. At toe-off, the tibia
changes direction again, to posterior translation entering the swing phase, and
concludes the gait cycle by translating anteriorly. Therefore, three anteroposterior
translation direction changes occur during one gait cycle. In a recent study by Gray et
al,12 using mobile biplane radiography, the translation pattern of the knee was more
consistent with a femoral rollback pattern throughout the flexion-extension excursion of
the knee. The translated distance was approximately 6.5 mm.
According to Koo and Andriacchi,13 the natural knee shows mostly lateral pivoting. More
internal/external rotation of the knee occurs during the swing phase than during the
stance phase of gait, covering a range of approximately 12°. For patients who undergo
TKA with a cruciate-retaining design, 13.9° (± 1.2°) was reported.14 The tibia exhibits
external rotation with respect to the femur entering swing and internally rotates at the
end of swing. These rotation patterns contradict the screw-home mechanism, which
specifies the internal tibial rotation with increasing knee flexion and external tibial
rotation on knee extension. These findings suggest that the knee is largely driven by
internal and external forces. Gray et al12 found the opposite and identified an
internal/external rotation pattern consistent with the screw-home mechanism. The
authors also found that, during gait, many of the secondary movements appear coupled
to the flexion/extension excursion of the joint, suggesting that the knee is guided by
internal constraints, such as ligaments and anatomic surface features.
Patellofemoral Kinematics
9/3/26, 7:30 AM
AAOS | Biomechanics of the Knee
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000552
5/19

Overview
In general, the patellofemoral joint can be viewed as a simple mechanical lever designed to
improve the function of the knee extensor muscle group (ie, the quadriceps).
Because of the large forces required by the knee extensors for functional activities, the patella
is subject to some of the greatest biomechanical forces in the body; some are measured as
high as eight times body weight.15
Common planes of motion: sagittal plane = flexion/extension; frontal plane = spin; transverse
plane = tilt.
Flexion ROM begins in an unstable position at full tibiofemoral extension, stabilized by joint
congruency after 20° of tibiofemoral flexion.
Patellar tracking is influenced by knee joint alignment, muscle forces, and passive stabilizing
forces.
Patellar tracking is defined by the quadriceps angle, or Q angle, a resultant load vector of the
tendency of the quadriceps and patellar tendons to pull the patella laterally16 (Figure 2).
Figure 2 Drawings depict patellar motion in a right knee. A = anterior, I = inferior, L = lateral, M =
medial, P = posterior, S = superior. (Adapted with permission from Katchburian MV, Bull AM, Shih
YF, Heatley FW, Amis AA: Measurement of patellar tracking: Assessment and analysis of the
literature. Clin Orthop Relat Res 2003;412:241-259.)

Overview
Lower limb alignment may have considerable effects on patellar tracking by changing the
relative position of the femoral trochlea or increasing the tension in the soft-tissue
restraints. The effect of altered tibial and femoral rotations on joint contact stress in the
patellofemoral joint has been explored extensively. Experimental studies have shown
the effect of increased internal femoral rotation or external tibial rotation on increased
lateral patellofemoral joint contact pressure.17,18 The natural anatomic alignment of the
bones of the femur, patella, and tibia can be used to measure the Q angle and visualize
the direction of pull of the quadriceps tendon. The Q angle is drawn by measuring a line
from the anterior superior iliac spine down to the center of the patella and then adding a
line from the center of the patella to the attachment of the patellar tendon at the tibial
9/3/26, 7:30 AM
AAOS | Biomechanics of the Knee
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000552
6/19

tuberosity. These two lines represent the force vectors applied at the patella by the
quadriceps and patellar tendons; the intersection of these lines is the Q angle (Figure 3).
Figure 3 Drawing of a hip and knee shows the direction of the quadriceps force vector (F
quadriceps) and the patellar tendon force vector (F patellar tendon), resulting in
anatomically-directed lateral force (F resultant). (Reproduced with permission from
Gustafson, JA: Development and Validation of a Kinematically-Driven Computational Model
of the Patellofemoral Joint. Pittsburgh, PA, University of Pittsburgh, 2017. Dissertation.).
The Q angle is a clinical measure commonly used in assessing the magnitude of laterally
directed forces acting on the patella from the resultant summation of the two force
vectors of the quadriceps and patellar tendons. This resulting lateral force commonly is
termed the law of valgus and has a considerable effect on the tracking of the patella
such that the lateral patellar facet receives 60% more force than the medial facet.19
Increases in the Q angle have been found to correspond with increasing joint contact
pressure in the lateral facet,20,21 which may place the patellofemoral joint at risk for
degeneration over time. In support of this effect, varus-valgus alignment has been
shown to correlate with compartment-specific patellofemoral osteoarthritis.22
Lower limb alignment is an important consideration in understanding patellofemoral
joint loading; however, static alignment does not necessarily imply poor dynamic loading
because it is possible for individuals to dynamically correct poor alignment via altered
muscular contraction strategies. The quadriceps mechanism may have a considerable
effect on patellar tracking. The role of the quadriceps during gait (or other weight-
bearing activities) is the effective shock absorption of the loads transmitted through the
tibiofemoral joint from heel contact. The patellofemoral joint is not engaged within the
trochlear groove until approximately 20° of flexion and, therefore, can be substantially
affected by the direction and magnitude of the quadriceps muscles. In particular, the
vastus medialis obliquus has been shown to be an important stabilizer for the patella in
cadaver model studies, providing medial restraint throughout motion.23,24
Understanding the effect of muscle loads on altered patellar motion and alignment
becomes more confounding in considering a disease state such as osteoarthritis
because quadriceps weakness is common in individuals with knee osteoarthritis.25,26
9/3/26, 7:30 AM
AAOS | Biomechanics of the Knee
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000552
7/19

The retinacular fibers of the patellofemoral joint provide a large portion of the passive
stability throughout knee ROM. The soft-tissue contributions from structures such as the
distal attachment site of the iliotibial band27 and from the joint capsule and ligaments
contribute to patellar stability. One of the most studied passive tissues is the medial
patellofemoral ligament (MPFL) because it is believed to play a major role in normal
tracking.28,29 The MPFL has been shown to account for approximately 50% to 60% of the
medial stabilization forces during knee flexion, centralizing the patella as it engages with
the trochlear groove.30 Injury to this structure may lead to increased lateral
patellofemoral tilting and potential increased stresses. Bony and articular geometry at
the patella and the distal femur also play an important role in patellar stability and
tracking.31 Studies have shown different patterns in patellar motion depending on
whether the tracking was relative to the femur32 or the femoral groove.33
During TKA, major considerations include correcting the alignment and positioning the
patella to maximize proper tracking because a large percentage of problems after TKA
are related to the patellofemoral articulation. External rotation of the femoral and tibial
components has been shown to aid in tracking because it may alleviate the natural
tendency of the patella to tilt laterally relative to the femur. Similarly, medialization of
the patellar button aids in patellar tracking and in the prevention of lateral subluxation
and dislocation.34 Another consideration for the patella during primary TKA is patellar
resurfacing because registry data have shown that routine retention of the native patella
during primary TKA is associated with a 20% to 30% increased risk for revision35
(Resource 2).
Knee Joint Kinetics
Kinetics is the field in classical mechanics that describes the relationship between motion and its
causes, specifically forces and moments.
Tibiofemoral Kinetics
The ground reaction force vector, arising during human locomotion, imposes external forces
and moments at the knee joint that must be balanced by a set of internal forces.
9/3/26, 7:30 AM
AAOS | Biomechanics of the Knee
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000552
8/19

These internal forces are generated by muscles, joint contact, and soft-tissue constraints.
Of these structures, the muscles are in the best position to resist the external moments
because they have sufficient lever arms, defined from their lines of action to the point of
contact at the joint.
Muscles may act synergistically or antagonistically to improve the stability of the joint. This
increases the joint contact forces.
Gait Kinetics
During walking, external moments arise in the sagittal plane, requiring flexor/extensor muscle
activity in the frontal plane and causing an uneven contact load distribution between the
medial and lateral plateau, and in the transverse plane, requiring secondary restraints (eg, the
menisci)
TKA must account for these requirements.

Gait Kinetics
Typically, during walking, an external flexion-extension moment occurs that tends to
extend the knee joint. To balance this moment internally, the flexor muscles have to
become active. As the knee moves into mid stance, the external moment reverses
direction, demanding the action of the extensor muscles. The external moment reverses
direction again during late mid stance, activating the flexor muscles. Finally, at toe-off,
the extensors become active again.
During walking, the adduction moment produces an asymmetric load distribution in the
frontal joint plane and forces the knee into varus. This process can be related to the
vector of the ground reaction force passing medial to the knee. The collateral ligaments
help to balance the loads between the medial and lateral condyles of the knee.
Therefore, proper tensioning of the collateral ligaments is absolutely critical for proper
function after TKA.
The observed moments during gait can be interpreted only in terms of net extensor and
net flexor demand. Muscles may act synergistically or antagonistically to improve the
stability of the joint. Antagonistic muscle activity increases the joint contact forces.
9/3/26, 7:30 AM
AAOS | Biomechanics of the Knee
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000552
9/19

Although low in magnitude, the transverse plane moments are difficult to balance by
muscle structures of the knee joint alone and require the assistance of the cruciate and
collateral ligaments. In the absence of these structures, patients may adapt their gait
and lower the moment.
Tibiofemoral Contact Forces
Numerous analytic and numeric models have been introduced for the natural and the
prosthetic human knee. Many of these models use external joint kinetics as input.
Calculated contact forces range from 1.7 to 3.5 body weight for walking and up to 5.4 body
weight for stair climbing.
Measured contact forces using instrumented prostheses range from 2.2 to 2.8 body weight for
walking. More vigorous activities increase contact forces to between 3.5 and 8 body weight.

Tibiofemoral Contact Forces
Major studies have been performed to directly measure knee forces with the help of
implants instrumented with strain gauges (Resource 3). D’Lima et al36 found axial
contact forces ranging from 2.2 to 2.8 times body weight. Higher forces are induced via
more vigorous activities.37 Axial forces increased to 3.5 to 8 times body weight for stair
ascent and downhill walking. These first-generation instrumented knee prostheses could
measure only axial contact forces. Heinlein et al38 developed a device capable of
measuring loads and moments for all six degrees of freedom. For level walking, axial
force measurements were similar to data found by D’Lima et al.36 Shear forces were
approximately 0.3 times body weight. During stair maneuvers, all force readings
increased by approximately 30%.
Instrumented knee forces are only available for a small subject cohort, and these forces
are not representative for all patients who undergo TKA. Therefore, mathematical
modeling of knee joints remains important. Only a few mathematical models assume
9/3/26, 7:30 AM
AAOS | Biomechanics of the Knee
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000552
10/19

friction of the joint surfaces. For TKA, shear forces play an important role in the failure
mechanisms of the joint. Shear forces can damage the polyethylene articulation and may
stress the underlying bone bed. Shear forces may arise from friction at the artificial
articulation, which may be 100-fold higher than that of cartilage.39
Patellofemoral Contact Forces
Patellofemoral forces are dictated by pulley mechanisms from the quadriceps and the patellar
tendon.
A complex interplay between increased patellofemoral forces and the bony contact area drives
patellofemoral stress.
Mechanisms of instability are largely driven by factors such as patella alta, high tibial-tubercle
to trochlear-groove distance, and femoral trochlea/patellar dysplasia.

Patellofemoral Contact Forces
Patellofemoral contact pressure results from the compressive forces applied by the
pulley-like mechanism from the quadriceps and the patellar tendon and the contact area
between the patella and the distal trochlea of the femur (Figure 4). The patellar cartilage
is subject to contact forces spanning sequentially from the inferior, middle, and superior
regions of the articular surface with increasing knee flexion. Contact between the distal
patella and the proximal femoral trochlea takes place at full extension. This contact
changes considerably at approximately 30° of tibiofemoral flexion, at which the patella
should be fully engaged within the trochlear groove.40 In addition, an increased lateral
translation of the patella occurs after it is engaged with the femoral trochlea. Although
the compressive joint contact forces are substantially increased in deeper flexion angles,
the congruency between the patellar cartilage and the femoral trochlea increase the
contact area, which leads to only marginal increases in stress. The ratio of these forces
to area directly affects the changes in pressure.
Figure 4 Schematic drawing of a knee shows the forces applied on the patella by the
9/3/26, 7:30 AM
AAOS | Biomechanics of the Knee
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000552
11/19

quadriceps muscle (FQ) and patellar tendon (Fp) and the resultant force (FR). F = force, P
= patellar tendon, Q = quadriceps, R = result. (Adapted from Mow VC, Flatow EL, Ateshian
GA: Biomechanics, in Buckwalter JA, Einhorn TA, Simon SR, eds: Orthopaedic Basic Science:
Biology and Biomechanics of the Musculoskeletal System, ed 2. Rosemont, IL, American
Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons, 2000, p 134.)
During weight bearing from full extension to 90° of flexion, the contact area and the
patellofemoral joint reaction force increase, with the force increasing substantially in
deeper flexion because of the increased tension in the quadriceps necessary to support
increasing flexion.41 Evidence on the pattern of the contact pressure with increasing
flexion during weight bearing has been mixed; however, the general consensus is that
contact pressure increases substantially in earlier flexion (0° to 30°) and increases
minimally in later flexion (30° to 90°) as the patella becomes fully engaged with the
trochlea and the contact area is maximized.19,20 The stress distributions occurring at
lower knee-flexion angles are important, particularly because these joint positions place
the patella at greater risk for maltracking from the increased effect of the active, passive,
and anatomic components on patellar motion.
Patellofemoral dislocation is estimated to account for 2% to 3% of all knee injuries. Girls
aged 10 to 17 years are the highest-risk group. Individuals who participate in pivoting
sports, have patella alta, have a high Q angle, have a high tibial-tubercle to trochlear-
groove distance, and/or have a dysplastic trochlea are at higher risk for instability and
dislocation. If managed nonsurgically, recurrent dislocations occur at an estimated rate
of 15% to 50%, depending on activity level and underlying risk factors.
Lateral dislocations occur if the MPFL, which is the primary medial patellar stabilizer,
ruptures (Figure 4). If the MPFL becomes incompetent, the patella tracks laterally and
may tilt. This likely increases the risk of dislocation and increases pressure on the lateral
patellar facet and the lateral trochlea, which may lead to arthritis. In addition, the bony
alignment, including the Q angle and the tibial-tubercle to trochlear-groove distance,
affect patellar tracking and stability.
Patients with patellar instability often have chondral or osteochondral injuries leading to
crepitus or locking or catching of the knee. After acute injury, patients may experience a
vague sense of instability of the knee, particularly in sports that require pivoting. On
9/3/26, 7:30 AM
AAOS | Biomechanics of the Knee
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000552
12/19

physical examination, the patella often is hypermobile and tracks laterally. Manual
lateral subluxation of the patella causes apprehension.
Patients with chronic instability and multiple dislocations often benefit from surgical
treatment; however, surgical treatment may be indicated in patients with a single, acute
dislocation, depending on the presence of a loose body requiring surgical management,
limb alignment, and the underlying risk of additional dislocations. Carefully selected
patients without a dislocation but who have chronic pain about the patella and distinct
clinical evidence of maltracking also may be candidates for surgical realignment if
nonsurgical treatment fails to afford adequate relief (Figure 4).
Wear in TKA
Historically, wear of polyethylene in TKA implants has been a common cause of implant failure
(Resource 3).
Delamination, defined as the formation of subsurface cracks in the polyethylene that
propagate to the surface over time, causes tibial plateau destruction.
Abrasive and adhesive wear, defined as the generation of submicron-sized polyethylene
wear particles during joint articulation, causes osteolysis of the periprosthetic bone and
subsequent loosening.
Joint kinematics and kinetics are important variables in determining wear.
New material formulations and sterilization techniques and implant design considerations
have reduced polyethylene wear drastically.
According to the 2020 Annual Report of the American Joint Replacement Registry,42 3.3% of
TKA implants were revised because of wear and osteolysis since 2012.
In addition, 24.2% of TKA implants were removed because they exhibited aseptic loosening,
which may result from progressive wear-particle–induced periprosthetic osteolysis.
Tribocorrosion is a material degradation process that results from the combined effect of
wear and corrosion.
It affects metals in the articulation and typically is confined to hard/hard bearing
combinations (eg, taper junctions or wear-through of polyethylene articular surfaces,
causing the femoral condyle to rub against the tibial base plate).
9/3/26, 7:30 AM
AAOS | Biomechanics of the Knee
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000552
13/19

It causes the release of metal ions and metal particles that may cause damage locally and
systemically.

Wear in TKA
Wear of the polyethylene tibial insert and the resulting mechanical and biologic
complications remain problematic and constitute a recognized cause of failure, limiting
long-term success. Although the precise mechanisms by which wear particles induce
periprosthetic osteolysis have not been fully elucidated and are an active area of
research, the particle characteristics, such as composition, size, shape, and overall
number (especially for those in the most biologically active submicrometer-size range)
are known to play a role in the cell and tissue response.43 Several factors may influence
the wear of ultra-high–molecular-weight polyethylene inserts. They can be grouped into
material factors (eg, type of resin, method of consolidation, shelf life, method of
sterilization, manufacturing process, level of oxidation), surgical technique factors (eg,
implant alignment, soft-tissue balance), and patient factors (eg, patient activity, gait
pattern).44
The relationship between wear and motion direction is nonlinear and has been
theoretically described. Because the molecular chains in the polyethylene surface layer
align along the direction of shear, more energy is required to rupture the molecules in
their longitudinal direction than perpendicularly. Therefore, polyethylene sheds more
particles if motion occurs in multiple directions. Kinematic and kinetic inputs have been
shown to affect the wear observed in actual patients and in joint simulators. For
example, McEwen et al45 showed that increased displacement and rotation during TKA
implant wear testing caused a substantial increase in the wear rate.
In summary, contact load and motion pathway affect implant wear and are influenced by
surgical technique, implant design, and patient-specific factors (Resource 4).
